chunks: Ahmad b. al-Hasan al-Qattan narrated to us. He said: Ahmad b. Yahya b. Zakariyya al-Qattan narrated to us. He said: Bakr b. Abdullah b. Habib narrated to us. He said: Ali b. Ziyad narrated to us. He said: al-Haytham b. Adi narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Yunus b. Abi Ishaq. He said: Abu al-Saqr narrated to us, from Adi b. Arta'a. He said:

Mu'awiya said one day to 'Amr b. al-'As: O Aba Abdillah! Which of us is more cunning? 'Amr said: I am [more cunning] in impulsiveness, and you are [more cunning] in deliberation. Mu'awiya said: You have judged in my favor over yourself, for I am more cunning than you in impulsiveness. 'Amr said: Then where was your cunning on the day you raised the codices?

He said: With that you have overcome me, O Aba Abdillah. Shall I not ask you about something in which you will be truthful with me? He said: By Allah, lying is repugnant, so ask about whatever you wish and I shall be truthful with you. He said: Did you cheat me after you counseled me? He said: No. He said: Rather, by Allah, you did cheat me. I am not saying in every instance, but in one particular instance. He said: And what instance is this?

He said: The day Ali b. Abi Talib challenged me to a duel and I consulted you. I said: What do you think, O Aba Abdillah? You said: A worthy and noble opponent. So you advised me to duel him while you knew who he was, and I knew then that you had cheated me. He said: O Commander of the Faithful, a man challenged you to duel him who was of great honor and immense standing. In dueling him you would have achieved one of two good outcomes: either you would kill him, which would have been the slaying of equals, and you would increase in honor upon your honor and have your kingdom to yourself; or you would hasten to the company of the martyrs and the righteous — and what excellent company they are.

Mu'awiya said: This is worse than the first. By Allah, I surely know that had I killed him I would have entered the Fire, and had he killed me I would have entered the Fire. 'Amr said to him: Then what drove you to fight him?! He said: Rulership has no blood bonds, and no one will hear this from me after you.

key_terms.الْحُسْنَيَيْن: the two good outcomes (victory or martyrdom)
key_terms.الْمَصَاحِف: codices/copies of the Quran (raised on spears at Siffin)
key_terms.الْمُلْكُ عَقِيمٌ: rulership has no blood bonds (i.e., power severs all ties)

ai.seo_question: What did Mu'awiya confess to 'Amr ibn al-'As about fighting Imam Ali?
ai.summary: This narrative from al-Amali of Shaykh al-Saduq records a private conversation between Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan and 'Amr ibn al-'As, two key political figures of early Islam. They candidly discuss their cunning, the raising of Quran codices at the Battle of Siffin (37 AH) as a ruse to halt fighting against Imam Ali (AS), and Mu'awiya's admission that 'Amr deceived him by encouraging him to accept Ali's duel challenge knowing Ali's unmatched prowess. Most remarkably, Mu'awiya confesses that he knew fighting Ali would lead him to Hellfire regardless of the outcome, but pursued power anyway, declaring 'Rulership has no blood bonds' — a damning self-indictment preserved in Shia historiography.
